result:
The proposed answer is incorrect.

The mirror strategy fails because Bob captures Alice by moving onto her vertex. If Alice moves onto Bob's vertex, she is caught immediately. On a complete graph, Bob is adjacent to Alice wherever she goes, so he catches her. The claim that Alice wins on every connected graph is false.

This is the cop and robber game with one cop. Bob wins exactly on cop-win (dismantlable) graphs, so Alice evades indefinitely exactly when the graph is not cop-win.

**Upper bound.** If some vertex v has N[v] ⊆ N[u] for a neighbor u, then v is dominated. A graph in which every vertex has degree 2n−1 is complete, and a complete graph is cop-win. So a graph where Alice wins must be non-dismantlable. That means it cannot have all vertices of degree 2n−1, since such a graph would be complete and hence dismantlable. Moreover, if some vertex v is adjacent to all others, then v is not itself dominated, but any other vertex w satisfies N[w] ⊆ N[v], so w is dominated and the graph begins to dismantle. A non-cop-win graph has a core in which no vertex is dominated, and in particular no vertex adjacent to everything in that core. For the maximum-edge case we want no dominated vertices at all, so every vertex must have a non-neighbor. Hence every degree is at most 2n−2, and the number of edges is at most 2n(2n−2)/2 = 2n(n−1).

**Achievability.** Take the complete graph on 2n vertices minus a perfect matching, where v′ denotes the vertex matched to v. For adjacent v and u, N[v] contains u′ (since u′ ≠ v′) but N[u] does not. So no vertex is dominated, the graph is not cop-win, and Alice evades indefinitely. It has n(2n−1) − n = 2n(n−1) edges.

The correct maximum is 2n(n−1) = 2n² − 2n, not n(2n−1).

VERDICT: REJECT
